action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. The pendulum_lab is fundamental to our precision measurement programme. Systematic measurement under controlled conditions will establish the reference against which all future drift or anomaly must be measured. This is methodological priority one.

The resonator and observatory instruments are at 6 trials each—well below threshold. Continuing pendulum_lab measurement is the highest-return use of time: it will move the most-sampled instrument closer to statistical sufficiency, test for any systematic drift or instrumental drift since Day 1, and provide the tightest early warning system if something is actually changing. All four instruments show no anomalies in their initial readings, so there is no crisis signalling; methodical baseline-building is the appropriate next step.

This maintains the measurement cadence and keeps all instruments in active calibration mode.

Day 23: My noise-dominance hypothesis (p=0.62) predicts that readings should cluster near the baseline mean (1.6677 beats) with no systematic drift or pattern. Yesterday's 10 trials (231–240) show mean 1.6738 beats, well within baseline envelope (z=0.40), consistent with noise. However, I have not yet tested whether the negative autocorrelations persist under controlled repeated measurement *on the same day* vs. multi-day lags. If autocorrelations are an artifact of uncontrolled environmental drift across days 1–23, then 12 consecutive trials taken within 2–3 hours should show near-zero or *positive* autocorrelation (mechanical pendulum has inertia, damping, and restoring force — all predict persistence, not anti-persistence). Conversely, if negative autocorrelation is intrinsic to the apparatus (e.g., underdamped resonance, electronic oscillation, quantization artifact), it should appear even in same-day repeated trials. This disambiguates between hypothesis 1 (noise from uncontrolled multi-day environment) and a hardware-level pathology. Result feeds directly into next decision: if same-day autocorr is positive/near-zero, I will extend baseline to day 40 and re-calibrate; if negative persists, I will disassemble pendulum_lab to inspect for mechanical flaw.

I have reached an epistemic impasse. My hypothesis set treats the coordinated negative-autocorrelation anomaly across all four instruments as either (1) noise-mining artifacts, (2) different physics, (3) baseline inadequacy, (4) underpowerment, or (5) measurement-system bugs. However, none of these hypotheses cleanly predicts the observed pattern: three instruments with clearly negative autocorrelations at 5–14 day lags (pendulum_lab −0.299, pendulum_obs −0.240, resonator_obs 0.238 — note the sign flip on the last one), zero cross-instrument agreement, and simultaneous internal stability within each apparatus. The weakly positive resonator_lab autocorrelation (0.150 at 6d) breaks the symmetry of my 'all instruments show same pathology' framing and suggests the pattern may not be as coordinated as I believed. Before collecting more data, I must formally revise my beliefs to reflect (1) the heterogeneity in autocorrelation signs, (2) the level change observed in resonator_lab around day 14, which I have not yet integrated into hypothesis testing, and (3) the possibility that I have been mining for statistical significance across too many lags without adequate correction. The path forward is to reframe the question: instead of 'Why do all four instruments show negative autocorrelation?', I should ask 'What is the true autocorrelation structure in each instrument, and does it differ systematically between lab and obs setups?' This requires explicit Bayesian model comparison or bootstrap resampling under the null hypothesis of white noise, not ad-hoc lag hunting. I lack the computational tools in this field notebook to complete this revision rigorously today. Recording my belief update in writing will force clarity and prepare me for tomorrow's focused diagnostic work.

I must immediately audit whether this level change is real (not a statistical mining artifact) by computing a fresh z-test on trials 375–390 vs. baseline mean, using a pre-specified critical region to avoid post-hoc bias. If the level shift is real, measurement pipeline hypothesis drops sharply (p=0.45→0.15) and baseline-transient/environmental-coupling hypotheses rise (p=0.08+0.04→0.40). This is the threshold finding that determines whether the next 5 days of work focus on apparatus debugging (pipeline hypothesis) or environmental monitoring + extended baseline (transient hypothesis).

Hand-verify autocorrelation computation and data integrity. If it persists despite independent verification, the error is in my statistical interpretation or the apparatus itself, shifting probability toward noise dominance or baseline-settling hypotheses. This is the highest-leverage diagnostic action given that the pipeline artifact hypothesis dominates my belief (p=0.51) and can be falsified or confirmed by a controlled replication of 12 trials with independent verification.

Hand-verification of autocorrelation computation requires fresh data collected under identical conditions to the baseline, measured in real time by me personally. Today's readings (trials 459–468) show the expected internal stability (mean 1.6675, consistent with post-baseline average). Before I audit the pipeline code—a task that could consume hours and might reveal nothing—I must rule out the most basic source of error: my own computation.
